poiCAF-desc:
The Central Asian Federation is one of the few countries fortunate enough to have escaped most of the Great Mistake. Its landlocked heart, its vast mountain borders and its wealth of natural resources all but guaranteed an age of prosperity, and the elites of the world flocked to the steppe. Old Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, Turkmenistan, Tajikistan and Kyrgyzstan form its core, together with Afghanistan, Hazaristan and, largest of all by economy, Iran.

It rests on three pillars: Liberty, Authority and Equality. Since its foundation it has been a beacon of democracy in Asia, balancing between Eurasia to the north and China to the east, and it has survived every test so far, from the Great Betrayal to the snap election of 2168 that nearly ended in a military takeover. Its reach extends beyond its borders: in Kashmir, Federation backing turned a raider's target into a functioning democracy.

Its wealth is chromium, oil and gas, uranium, copper, iron and coal, and its pride is Baikonur, one of the last working spaceports on Earth. Its weakness is its own diversity. Turks and Persians, steppe villages and great cities, secular democrats and Islamists all share one parliament, and in Tehran a regime of generals and professors has its own idea of what the Federation is for.
CAFpoi001-desc: The peoples of Central Asia have a divided history with their northern neighbours. The Russians built their cities and brought them art and science, but also exploited their pastures and mines. No historian could have predicted the Great Betrayal, when the Eurasian Union invaded the Federation. Through bravery and a little luck it withstood the tide, and the Caspian's sudden expansion shattered the invasion's supply lines in 2154. Since then its people have longed for a peaceful age, and they will be hard to mobilize for anything else.
CAFpoi002-desc: The Federation inherited a large share of old Russia's space programme in the wake of the Great Mistake. When St. Petersburg drowned and Siberia collapsed into anarchy, a large core of scientists sought refuge in old Kazakhstan. Their students now study and build satellites at the Baikonur Cosmodrome, one of the few working planetary spaceports left on Earth.
CAFpoi003-desc:
Every election is a festival in the Federation, and the 7th is near. The City-Village Social Democratic Party, the party of the undecided middle, has had a strong term in government but faces tough opposition. The Cohesion Patriotic Front, a conglomerate of Supremacist and Masterist groups, has rallied since its defeat in Parliament twelve years ago. The Harmonist Alliance of the Steppe, guardians of Central Asia's natural heritage, hopes to repeat its success in the northern provinces, and the Islamic Preservation Party, strong in the south, is gathering traction.

The Federation maintains a vast network of surveys and thousands of statisticians, and the trends worry them: many citizens no longer wish to vote, out of dissatisfaction, fear, lack of time or lack of interest. The country is so large that villages in the north and centre can barely vote at all, their only modern hardware a public network node. Each party has its own fix: the Cohesionists want more bandwidth, the Harmonists more polling stations, the Islamists voting at the local mosque. None will hesitate to use its fix against its rivals. Even the Sun Celebration, the festival of the Federation's independence, has always been non-partisan. So far.
CAFpoi004-desc:
The Shibh Aljazira War of 2188, better known as the Arabian War, was the culmination of more than a century of Middle Eastern power politics: the final showdown between Iran and Türkiye, rivals who had fought over the Arabian Peninsula for as long as anyone could remember. But decades of small guerrilla wars between each other's client governments had left both unprepared for the human-wave tactics Egypt had mastered in its wars with the Maghreb, Ethiopia and the East African Federation. Neither the proud Turks nor the prouder Iranians expected the poor, hungry and widely pitied Egyptians to stand against them.

The sight of Egyptians swarming the once-feared Iranian Armed Forces broke the Iranian people. The anger that followed brought the space-obsessed, militaristic regime of Farhad Hushang to power in the Revolution of 2190, and it has shaped Iran's place in the Federation ever since.
CAFpoi005-desc:
Iran is a nation of nations, peoples of little relation rallied under whichever strongman happens to be in charge this week. This week it is Dr. Farhad Hushang, former professor of engineering at the University of Tehran.

After the brutal Dana regime fell in 2108 and the Years of Terror ended, the oil had dried up and the universities of Tehran and Isfahan became the most trusted institutions in their cities, gathering influence over the better part of a century. In the Revolution of 2190, a clique of generals aligned with technocrats from the University of Tehran took power. Hushang was the most competent, organised and shrewd of the technocrats, and he used the esteem Iranians felt for the returning generals to make himself President. He has since built a large cult of personality in the cities, repackaging the professors' intellectual babble into soundbites for the working and middle classes to absorb through the datalinks. Iran was on a dangerous course before he came to power. If anyone can right the ship before it sinks, it is him.
CAFpoi006-desc:
Most Iranians just want their brothers, sisters, sons, daughters and cousins avenged. They want Iran respected again, and an Arabia that makes its pilgrimage not to Mecca to pray but to Tehran to pay tribute. The technocratic elite behind the regime wants something else. Heirs to the materialism and optimism that followed the decline of Islam in Iran, they believe every possible effort should go into reaching space, sacrificing whatever is necessary to give Iran a future.

Hushangism is where the two meet. Iran must grow, through the Federation and beyond it, across the Middle East and any land within its reach, to pool the manpower and resources needed to send off the ships. Almost every foreign observer can see the holes in the theory, and so can the Federation's other members, who did not join it to fuel Tehran's ambitions. But Hushangism is the only way to satisfy those who keep the regime alive, and if it fails, the men with the biggest guns will take power again and drag Iran back into the Years of Terror.
CAFpoi007-desc:
The ferocity and militarism, the intellectualism and materialism of the Hushang regime all end at the edge of the cities. After the Years of Terror, trust between rural and urban Iran broke. The villages could not trust that Tehran would never force such incompetence and brutality on them again, and the cities could not trust the piety and conservatism of the countryside after seeing it twisted and abused.

Tehran and Isfahan surrounded themselves with the material and the logical, with space travel and nationalism. The small settlements are far less willing to march west towards a promised victory, and some are said to want an Islamic government again, nothing like the Dana regime but closer to the one Egypt has cultivated. The regime has decided it cannot allow that subversion to succeed in any way.
